items.abstract:
<jats:p>The rapid digitalization of financial services has significantly increased the scale and complexity of fraudulent activities across financial institutions. Conventional fraud detection systems, primarily based on rule-based mechanisms and tabular machine learning models, often fail to identify sophisticated and interconnected fraud schemes spanning multiple institutions. Furthermore, increasing regulatory requirements regarding transparency and data privacy restrict direct sharing of financial transaction data among organizations. This study proposes a privacy-preserving and adaptive fraud detection framework that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Federated Learning (FL), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to enable collaborative fraud detection across institutions without compromising sensitive customer information.

The proposed framework models financial ecosystems as distributed heterogeneous graphs consisting of accounts, merchants, devices, and transactional relationships. A federated graph learning mechanism enables participating institutions to collaboratively train fraud detection models while preserving local data ownership. To address the interpretability limitations of deep learning systems in highly regulated financial environments, XAI techniques are integrated to provide transparent explanations for fraud predictions at transaction, account, and network levels. Additionally, adaptive learning strategies are incorporated to address evolving fraud patterns and concept drift over time.

The study presents the conceptual architecture, methodological framework, privacy-preserving mechanisms, explainability integration, and evaluation strategy for the proposed system. The framework aims to improve fraud detection accuracy, enhance regulatory compliance, and facilitate collaborative intelligence sharing among financial institutions while maintaining strict privacy guarantees.</jats:p>
title: Graph Neural Network (GNN) and XAI for Adaptive, Cross-Institutional Fraud Detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Nowadays, digital platforms have increasingly relied on recommendation systems to connect users with relevant products and services. However, these systems often operate in environments vulnerable to major external shocks. Such shocks can reshape user preferences, item characteristics, and interaction patterns, creating a critical challenge for platforms seeking to maintain effective recommendation. In such settings, interactions accumulated before the shock contain useful collaborative signals but may also include outdated information, whereas interactions observed afterward reflect emerging behaviors but are often too sparse for recommendation. How to selectively reuse historical knowledge while adapting to post-shock changes remains insufficiently studied. To address this research gap, we formulate the cross-phase recommendation problem and propose an adaptive graph neural network framework for resilient recommendation under external shocks, which adapts historical knowledge at both the representation and interaction levels. Specifically, we develop a personalized knowledge transfer module that learns user- and item-specific gates to determine how much historical information should be retained and adapted after the shock. We further design a personalized graph augmentation module that selectively incorporates informative historical interactions into the sparse graph after the shock. Comprehensive experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms other alternatives. Its superiority remains consistent across cities, evaluation metrics, and test months. The temporal results also show that it recovers rapidly from the initial performance decline and sustains strong recommendation performance over an extended period.</jats:p>
title: Resilient Cross-Phase Recommendation: An Adaptive Graph Neural Network Framework

items.abstract: <jats:p>Critical infrastructure networks face increasingly sophisticated cyber threats that traditional detection methods struggle to identify in real-time. This paper presents AGNN-TID (Adaptive Graph Neural Network for Threat Intelligence and Detection), a novel framework that models infrastructure systems as dynamic temporal graphs and employs attention-based graph neural networks to detect anomalous patterns indicative of cyberattacks. Unlike existing approaches that treat network elements independently, AGNN-TID captures spatial relationships between infrastructure components and temporal evolution of attack patterns simultaneously. We introduce a new multi-scale attention mechanism that adapts to infrastructure topology changes and learns hierarchical threat representations. The framework incorporates a novel loss function combining supervised classification with unsupervised anomaly detection, enabling effective learning even with limited labeled attack data. Extensive evaluation on three datasets-NSL-KDD, CICIDS2017, and a newly collected Australian critical infrastructure dataset (AUS-CII-2024)-demonstrates that AGNN-TID achieves 96.8% detection accuracy with2.3% false positive rate, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 8.4% in F1-score while reducing detection latency to under 180ms. The framework successfully detected zero-day attack patterns in our infrastructure testbed that signature-based systems missed entirely. Mathematical analysis proves the convergence properties of our training algorithm and establishes theoretical bounds on detection performance. Our code and AUS-CII-2024 dataset are publicly available to enable reproducibility and future research.</jats:p>
title: Adaptive Graph Neural Network Framework for Real-Time Threat Detection in Critical Infrastructure Networks

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Allosteric communication is essential to protein function, facilitating the dynamic regulation of biological responses through the propagation of structural and dynamic changes between regulatory and effector sites in response to stimuli. Traditional approaches to studying protein allostery often rely on static protein structures or abstract representations involving fully connected interaction graphs, which do not capture the temporal and state-dependent nature of these dynamic systems. Here, we introduce AlloPool, a graph neural network (GNN)-based model that iteratively prunes residue interactions to identify minimal, time-dependent interaction networks that govern long-range structural and dynamic responses to chemical or mechanical stimuli. Using temporal attention and graph aggregation, AlloPool accounts for evolving protein conformations in both molecular dynamics (MD) and steered MD (SMD) simulations to predict MD and SMD trajectories. We validate AlloPool on the Pin-1 protein and the ADGRG1 and B1AR receptors, showcasing its ability to accurately recapitulate protein motions, infer allosteric communication pathways, and identify critical allosteric sites. Additionally, AlloPool identifies force-dependent changes in GAIN domain structure and reconstructs directed information flow under mechanical load. Comparative analyses indicate that AlloPool outperforms existing models in MD and SMD trajectory reconstruction, presenting a new framework for analyzing force- and ligand-induced allosteric motions. This work advances the modeling of allosteric systems and offers broad potential for applications in drug discovery, synthetic biology, and protein engineering.</jats:p>
title: AlloPool: An Adaptive Graph Neural Network for Dynamic Allosteric Network Prediction in Protein Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Adaptive and deployable structures are increasingly important in modern engineering systems including aerospace mechanisms, soft robotics, deployable space structures, and responsive architectural components where lightweight and reconfigurable designs must operate reliably under varying loads and environmental conditions. Origami-inspired engineering structures provide a promising solution by enabling foldable geometries capable of large and controllable shape transformations while using minimal material and maintaining structural efficiency. However, optimising origami crease patterns is a computationally challenging task because the configuration space defined by fold angles, geometric constraints, and material properties is highly nonlinear, high-dimensional, and often non-convex. Traditional optimisation approaches such as gradient-based methods or evolutionary algorithms frequently struggle to efficiently explore this complex design space and may converge to suboptimal folding configurations. In this work, we propose a hybrid Origami-Quantum Graph Neural Network (OQ-GNN) framework for adaptive structural optimisation of origami-based systems. In the proposed approach, origami crease patterns are represented as graphs in which nodes correspond to fold joints and store structural attributes such as fold angles, crease types, and material stiffness, while edges represent crease connectivity and geometric constraints between folds. A graph neural network performs message passing across the crease network to capture relational structural interactions and learn expressive embeddings that describe the global folding configuration. These learned representations are then processed by a quantum-inspired amplitude exploration module that encodes candidate structural states using complex-valued probability amplitudes, enabling simultaneous exploration of multiple design configurations through a superposition-like sampling mechanism implemented entirely on classical hardware. Experimental evaluation on a dataset of procedurally generated origami crease patterns with finite-element-based structural responses demonstrates that the proposed method achieves improved optimisation accuracy, reduced structural stress, and faster convergence compared with classical optimisation baselines and standard graph neural network approaches. The results suggest that combining graph-based structural learning with quantum-inspired probabilistic exploration provides an effective and scalable strategy for the design and optimisation of adaptive origami engineering structures.</jats:p>
title: A Hybrid Origami-Quantum Graph Neural Network Framework for Adaptive Structural Design and Optimisation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate forecasting of wind power is essential for maintaining the stability and efficiency of power networks as renewable energy sources become more integrated. This study proposes a multilevel spatial-temporal graph convolution network (MLAGCN) for wind power forecasting. The framework combines a multilevel adaptive graph convolution (MLAGC) and a lightweight temporal transformer (LWTT) to jointly model complex spatial-temporal relationships in wind power data. MLAGC is constructed using three adaptive graphs: a local-aware graph, a global-aware graph, and a structure-aware graph. These components form a flexible graph structure that effectively represents dynamic spatial interactions while LWTT learns short- and long-term sequential patterns. Experiments on real wind farm datasets demonstrated that the proposed model outperforms existing baselines. The model achieved an improved prediction accuracy and generalization, as indicated by a lower score of 43.44, mean absolute error (38.83), root mean square error (48.05) and a forecast loss of 0.22. These results demonstrates the effectiveness of temporal modeling and multilevel attention-based adaptive graph learning for high-resolution wind power forecasting.</jats:p>
title: Wind Power Forecast Using Multilevel Adaptive Graph Convolution Neural Network

items.abstract: Similar approaches are very useful in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks in which: a flood of traffic and events occurs, especially in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as congestion control can have a huge impact in efficient traffic field and communication. The existing congestion control mechanisms are not suitable for this type of dynamic network topology and vehicle mobility. In response to these challenges, we propose an Adaptive Multi-Agent Graph Neural Network (AMAGNN), which utilizes graph neural networks (GNNs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for congestion control in vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs). Institute, “AMAGNN models VANETs as dynamic graphs, with vehicles being intelligent agents that cooperatively learn to optimize data propagation and alleviate network congestion. Optimizes for scalability and adaptability by dynamically responding to network topology changes and traffic density variation. Results show that the proposed AMAGNN model outperforms current practices in congestion control for VANETs on all the key performance metrics. It attains Packet Delivery Ratio (92.5%), lowest delay (28.4 ms), and maximum throughput (275.6 kbps) which shows reliability and efficiency in communication. It also achieves the lowest congestion level (0.35) and average waiting time (0.31 s), highlighting its ability to reduce traffic and delay. AMAGNN achieves the best performance, compared with methods such as GCN-RL, DQN Adaptive, and MA-PPO, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive multi-agent graph neural networks in the ever-changing vehicular environment.
title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Graph Neural Network (AMAGNN) for Congestion Control in VANET

<jats:p>Objectives: To propose a novel neural network-based load balancing approach for energy-efficient and congestion-aware routing in large-scale wireless sensor network (WSN) environments. The key objective is to develop intelligent routing that is capable of learning node-level interactions and predicting network load conditions to enhance routing efficiency, traffic fairness, and network lifetime. Methods: The Adaptive Graph Neural Network-Based Load Balancing (AGNN-LB) method treats wireless sensor networks as graphs comprised of sensor nodes and links as vertices (V) and edges (E), respectively. Node attributes such as residual energy, queue length, traffic rate, node degree, transmission delay, congestion level, and link quality are extracted by a graph feature extraction layer. The adaptive graph convolution layers learn the latent spatial correlations among neighboring nodes and encode spatial node embeddings. Subsequently, the dynamic load balancing engine predicts the node loads and re-routes network traffic based on the learned graph embedding. The AGNN-WSN2026 dataset containing 1,000 samples of graph-enabled sensor nodes is utilized for training and evaluating the performance. The proposed AGNN-LB is compared against baseline models such as GW-LBC and DBlock-RLB. The implementation is done using PyTorch for GNN development, NS-3 for network simulation, and Python for performance evaluation and statistical analysis. Findings: The simulation results reveal that AGNN-LB shows an outstanding performance, outperforming baseline models in energy efficiency with 96.8%, 97.4% network lifetime and a load balancing index of 96.5%, whereas it achieves a lower congestion level of 4.2% and end-to-end delay of 18.6 ms under different network environments. Novelty: The model stands as a unique design that combines AGNN with load balancing decision-making for wireless sensor networks (WSNs). Unlike typical clustering and routing schemes, the new design learns the spatial dependency among nodes as well as congestion propagation behavior to facilitate topology-aware, energy-aware, and intelligent traffic distribution for future autonomous WSNs.

Keywords: Wireless Sensor Networks, Graph Neural Networks, Load-Balancing Model, Energy Efficiency, Congestion-Aware WSNs</jats:p>
title: AGNN-LB: Adaptive Graph Neural Network Based Load Balancing for Energy Efficient and Congestion Aware Wireless Sensor Networks
